title: Schools, but not states, should ban phones
author: Michael J. Petrilli
summary: Mike Petrilli says he is a hawk on school technology: he favors bell-to-bell phone bans and would also curtail Chromebooks and much other classroom tech. Yet he is unsure that states should mandate such bans, since district autonomy, charter freedom and private school independence all come into play. He widens the question to the recurring tension in American education between local control and evidence-based mandates, noting that conservatives who prize local control often reach for bans when they love or loathe a practice. He closes by asking readers for a defining principle that avoids state micromanagement while still pushing schools toward evidence-based practice. The rest of the post is a news roundup that is not part of the core argument.
points: Petrilli supports bell-to-bell phone bans and a broader pullback on Chromebooks and classroom devices, treating phones as classroom cancer.
He questions whether the same logic justifies state mandates over districts, charters and private schools.
He frames phone bans as one case of the perennial local-control versus state-mandate tension, alongside the science of reading and advanced-class enrollment.
He notes conservatives invoke local control until a policy they love or hate arrives, then reach for mandates.
He asks for a defining principle that discourages state micromanagement while still promoting evidence-based practice.
quotes: I like phone bans. I think both common sense and the early evidence indicate that smartphones are, as Robert Pondiscio has said, “classroom cancer.” We don’t let kids smoke in school anymore, and we shouldn’t give them access to distraction devices while they are supposed to be learning.

I even like bell-to-bell bans (rather than just classroom bans), so that kids will be more likely to talk to one another in the hallway and cafeteria, and to give their brains a nice long break from the stimulating effects of Screenworld.

In fact, cellphone bans are not enough. We also need to curtail the Chromebooks and most other classroom tech. A Chromebook—or especially a Macbook—can easily serve as a big-old phone, allowing kids to cheat, text, and even gamble on sports (happening at my kids’ high school, I hear!) instead of listening to their teacher.

Some districts have gone heavy into digital learning. Should they be allowed to opt out of these bans? Should charter schools have to abide by such prohibitions, even though this is the sort of top-down regulation from which they are supposed to enjoy autonomy?
These sorts of questions are perennial ones for the American education system, given its fragmentation and historical commitment to local control.

We conservatives in particular like to talk about states’ rights and local control—except when we bump up against a policy or practice that we love or hate. And then we, too, can’t help but turn to mandates or bans.
